utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-84-T, the Prosecutor versus Ramush Haradinaj et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before we give you, Mr. Re, an opportunity to continue the examination-in-chief of the witness, I'd like to deal briefly with a few procedural matters. First of all, the Chamber received notice that, I think it was approximately one hour ago, that you had filed a motion to have exhibits added to the exhibit list. Let me first ask: I have not -- it was a courtesy copy that was sent to the Chamber's staff without attachments. First of all, has the Defence received that motion?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see two times nodding yes, affirming Mr. Emmerson. Would you like to respond to it?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I have no objection to those documents being added to the exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. The same is true for other counsel? I see again two times nodding yes, which makes it three, so that matter has been then dealt with. I would like to, first of all, give a decision -- well, here it was a decision on what I would call a suggestion or a proposal; that is, your proposal of yesterday, Mr. Re, to move forward the testimony of Witness 19, which was originally scheduled for a later date in this trial, and your suggestion was that we'd hear that witness on this Friday. The Defence objected to the proposal on the grounds that it was not informed on time about the date of Witness 19's testimony, and that it therefore could not properly prepare for that witness. In light of these submissions, the Chamber decides that the Defence would be put at a disadvantage if Witness 19 was to be heard on Friday; and, therefore, the proposal by the Prosecution is rejected. I would like to go into private session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. These were, as far as I'm concerned, the procedural issues to be raised at this very moment. So, therefore, we are now ready, I take it -- Mr. Re, is the Prosecution ready to call Ms. Andjelkovic to continue the examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm ready subject to the matter of amending the exhibit list. I understand the Defence has indicated they don't propose -- they don't oppose it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re, you're perfectly right. The Chamber should have delivered a decision before inviting you to call Ms. Andjelkovic. In view of your request and in view of the fact that the Prosecution does not oppose granting your request, the request is hereby granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank Your Honour. I'd just indicate that in relation to the way I'd propose proceeding is we -- to put this on the record: The Prosecution, last night, delved further into the issues relating to the translation of the diaries. We communicated with the Trial Chamber's legal officer and with Defence counsel last night and this afternoon. What we have discovered, our inquiries have revealed, is that in relation to volume 2, that they were translated in batches and they weren't merged into one document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Some from the B/C/S; other from the Latin script. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Last night -- very late last night, the translator put them all together and identified them, cross-matched that volume against the ERN of the original. The two translators were working on the other volume, which was volume 1, the first notebook. The problem there is that -- well, it wasn't a problem at the time; it is a problem now. When it was translated in-house, we used someone who was a specialist in Cyrillic to do the Cyrillic, and one someone who was a specialist in Latin writing to do the Latin. It was done years ago, and the two were never put back together until day. They have now been merged together into the one document, identifying against the ERN in the original. And where there are gaps in the translation, the selective translations, the translator has identified those. So we will seek leave or substitute those for whichever ones are in e-court at the moment. There is one further matter I must alert the Trial Chamber to which isn't fully resolved at the moment. The translator informed me, I think it was basically a couple of hours ago, that she had discovered that some of the pages, when they were put into her -- I think we've notified the Chamber and the Defence of this, were put in a -- were not copied in -- all of them, in the correct order and some of them are out of sequence; that is, the original documents were photo -- were copied into the evidence collection but not necessarily in the correct page number. The ERNs are sequential, but the pages are not. I'm attempting -- I think the translator is trying to identify which are out of order at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I can imagine, Mr. Re, that in view of the concerns expressed by the Defence on chronology, that this is a -- I mean, if it's one page which is not dealt with in the testimony, I can imagine that it would not cause major problems. But if, of course, if the -- it very much depends on how serious the problem is. Is it one page moved to a different place or is it -- and is that clearly visible on the basis of its content? Then I can imagine that we, or at least you and the Defence, could manage and the Trial Chamber could finally manage the matter. But if it is just a matter of throwing them all from the stairs and see which one is first down and then put them in that order, then, of course, we would have a greater problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm told by our case manager, Mr. Smith, that we have disclosed - it was only I'm told, half an hour ago - the re-arranged version in the order in which it actually appears in the notebooks. There was confusion this morning. I think we got both of them from the translator; we did them both ways. But the message was not properly communicated to disclose it. And I think the Defence and the Chambers now have two copies of the second volume; one in the correct order it appears in the original, and the second one in the order it appears in the ERN of the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the best copy to consult is the one with not subsequent ERN numbers, because subsequent ERN numbers means mixed-up original pages?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's correct, the one with mixed up -- the one with sequential ERNs is mixed-up originals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, as far as translation is concerned, is there a subsequent translation of the copy with the non-subsequent ERN numbers? I mean, the original order.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you have two versions, is the version which gives the right chronology, therefore, not reflecting subsequent ERN numbers? Do we have a translation which follows that original order?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. That was the one I was referring to a moment ago that we disclosed about -- earlier this afternoon, about half an hour ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Any need to comment on that, Mr. Emmerson?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, no. The re-ordered version of what is, in fact, the first notebook - I think Mr. Re said the second - the first notebook was disclosed today --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Re, first notebook?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I agree. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The second notebook was disclosed late last night. So that the first notebook is disclosed today. The second version of that we understand now to be in chronological order. It was e-mailed at 11 minutes past 2.00 this afternoon. And so given that Your Honours have already indicated that there will be sufficient time between examination-in-chief and cross-examination for the Defence to assimilate the order and material, and transfer the references to their notes, then there's no objection so far as we are concerned. May I simply register one very small point. Because of the way this matter has been handled, I hope we will be forgiven during cross-examination for using only the translations rather than being in a position, as Judge Hoepfel indicated would obviously be easier for the witness in principle, of being able with ease, to move between the original and the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course. If there would be really need for the witness to consult the original, then they'll find a way out. Yes. I think in modern terminology, this is called a learning moment, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Maybe just one other matter, which is this: Mr. Re suggested substituting the new translations for the existing exhibit numbers. The only reason I rise to my feet is because we're all aware that the way the transcript works is that there is a direct hyperlink between any reference by the court officer to the Exhibit P1 and the relevant passage that is being used in the course of examination, and the danger of substitution, as opposed to giving fresh exhibit numbers, is that we'll have a different document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It might be a solution that the MFI number, as we have it now, never changes its status, but that we know exactly what has been tendered. And that we would not then substitute the translation with anything else, but that we get in the right chronology with a proper translation a new exhibit number, and that the other is there to be consulted, if need be, but it's not in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think that may be better in the long run, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For those who will try to resolve these puzzles at a later stage. Mr. Re, we return to the moment where I said, Are you ready to continue the examination-in-chief of --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I am. If I could just explain very briefly how I would propose to conclude this witness' evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I propose to do it in the following manner: With the now-approved amendments to the exhibit list -- and I say, frankly, the Prosecution should have done it the other way around; we should have started with the "Spotlight" reports, using the incident -- the incident reports, which were the source material for the "Spotlight" reports, and having the diaries for the source material if necessary for the witness to refer to. And all I can do is apologise for the confusion and mix-up to my colleagues and the Trial Chamber for what has occurred here. Having now, as far as -- as much as I can in the available time, I think, rectified the situation, what I would propose to do is to take the witness to the incident reports and ask her to identify which of those are hers, so they're on the record, and take her to the "Spotlight" reports, asking her to identify which parts of the reports relate to her. And with a later witness, I will go into more detail in relation to the "Spotlight" reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's good to know how you intend to proceed, and if there's any objection, I expect the Defence to come with the objection, if you're examining the witness. Then, Madam Usher, would you please escort the witness into the courtroom; the witness being Ms. Andjelkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can I also indicate, E-court is, of course, a wonderful technological invention and it works fabulously well for tendering documents. But if witnesses are being shown a voluminous quantity, it may be easier to show them the documents in a folder and refer to the page in e-court. We have prepared a folder of the "Spotlight" reports and the incident reports, which I can distribute to the Bench and to the Defence and to the witness, which may make things smoother and quicker for the witness to go through in the time available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I must admit that at this very moment, my major concern would be whether the witness sees the same as we have on our screen. That is of some concern. And I think, as a matter of fact, managing the screen is relatively simple. So to the extent possible, I would invite you, Mr. Re, to use the screen, as much as possible, because one thing is for sure, that that's the same everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The only difficulty is the translations aren't in e-court yet, but the incident reports are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then we'll -- to that extent, we'll work, then, on the basis of hard copies. Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was not very polite, Ms. Andjelkovic, when you came in and when we just continued our discussions. Apologies for that. Thank you for coming back to the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Andjelkovic, you are still bound by the solemn declaration you have given yesterday at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Re will now continue his examination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, please proceed and distribute whatever there is to be distributed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ms. Andjelkovic.

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What I want to do this afternoon is -- yesterday, you referred to -- you gave an amount of evidence about your trips to Kosovo in March and April 1998 as a human rights field worker for the Humanitarian Law Centre in Belgrade. You told the Trial Chamber that you had interviewed various people, mainly ethnic Serbs, on the ground in various villages. You had put your observations into notebooks, and the notebooks you typed into reports, and the reports later were used in publications of the Humanitarian Law Centre. Since you were here last night, we have - that is, the Prosecution - has located a number of incident reports provided by the Humanitarian Law Centre. What I would like you to do is if I could hand you this folder, and the folder contains the English translations of your diaries, volumes 1 and 2, "Spotlight" reports number 26 and 27, and the incident reports. I've opened up the page of the incident report and I just want you, while I'm handing the others around the courtroom, to have a look through those incident reports and, just to yourself, identify any which you may have had a hand in, but not aloud just yet because I'll be doing something administratively.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: While the witness is looking at that, could these, please, be distributed around the court to the Bench and to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Ms. Andjelkovic, I'll just give you some yellow stickers or little post-it notes, which may assist you in marking any documents which are yours.

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, before Mr. Re continues, from a brief perusal of the incident reports contained in the file, which of course isn't paginated so I'm not in a position to refer you to particular pages, but you will find that there are, roughly halfway through, there's a page which says: "This job requires more memory than is available in this printer." And what's happened is that the report that immediately precedes that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just quickly try to guide us. It's not easy, I do understand, but is it in the first half, second half?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It's -- if I find the -- if I -- yes, if I -- it's about -- well, do Your Honours see that the green sheets separate the different sections?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The very final section of the "Spotlight" reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Final section, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Of those printed. Then Your Honour has the dividing line exactly, and then before that, between that and the immediately preceding green sheet, are the incident reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And I say roughly about between a quarter and a third of the way in, you will find an incident report which has a reference number, but it's probably not the easiest thing to find. They all have the same appearance. But you may find the page that looks like this and a page following it that looks like this. Now, I don't know how widespread the problem may be, but the paper copy is not, at least in that respect --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see the page where in the middle it appears: "The job requires more memory than is available. Try one or more of the following and print again."

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: If Your Honour sees the page before, the report before is cut in half, the version that we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is a statement -- yes, the page contains a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Which stops mid-sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: We obviously have -- the e-court system and the Defence have the full statement. It may be that there are other documents in this bundle for which that problem arises; I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's being rectified as we speak. You might have noticed that the case manager came in late with all of these.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It wasn't properly checked before we brought it in. New copies of this, with the ERNs on the top, will be here very, very shortly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let us see. We at least know there are some pages which contain rather information, and any whether relevant information for this case. Again, Ms. Andjelkovic, you're again a bit of a victim of these technical problems; but Mr. Re will ask you, I take it, whether you were able to find what he asked you to find.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Ms. Andjelkovic, have you had a chance to go through and -- all I want you to do at the moment - I can see you've got some yellow stickers on the documents in front of you - I'd just wish for you to, first of all, tell the Court the first one. By incident report, there should be a date -- sorry, excuse me. To properly lay the foundation here, I'll go back. Yesterday, you referred in your evidence to incident -- to reports written as a result of your investigations in the field. Are these the reports that you and your colleagues typed up after interviewing the people in the field?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They pretty much look like this, except I have to say I don't remember this -- the logo, but that's the only change. Everything else is pretty much the same. This was the form.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: They're in English. Did you write them in English at the time?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The first one in this bundle, which has an ERN of K0577171 in the copy I have, but not the copy you have, has a date of report of the 27th [Realtime transcript read in error "22nd"] of April, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is that one which you took?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What's the next one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Is it the 22nd or the 27th?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: What did you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The 27th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For the record, it was the 22nd. I think the confusion might come from that the report seems to bare the date of the is 27th, and the incident is described as taking place on the 22nd. Your microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just for the sake of completeness, Your Honours we will see that there is a list of information; one of which is witness, and the date of interview appears under that as the 25th. So this document refers to an interview on the 25th about an incident on the 22nd which is filed in a report on the 27th. That's the pattern that follows through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's clear. Mr. Re, please proceed. Mr. Re, if you're referring to documents, you have now identified it by the date of the document, being the 27th of April; the date of the incident being the 22nd of April -- 22nd of April. From what I see the next one relates -- is a document dated the 22nd of April, and the incident referred to is also the 22nd of April. So would you please be more precise in identifying your documents, either by names or anything else. I also see that there is a kind of a file number on top, the first one being e20glodj.doc; the second in the list, e19glodj.doc; the third one, e18glodj.doc. That might be a better way of referring to the incident reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I am going to have to wait until the copies of the ERNs arrive. It appears that, unfortunately, the copy which you have is out of order ERN order. I'll have to -- I'll have to move to something else. I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then please do as you deem fit.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'll come back to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Ms. Andjelkovic, while we're waiting for the other copy to arrive, I want to take you to two "Spotlight" reports, which are at the very back of that bundle which you have there. The first one is "Spotlight" report number 26. I want you just to have a brief look at that, please. Now, "Spotlight" report number 26 is headed, "Kosovo Human Rights in Times of Armed Conflict," and was published by the Humanitarian Law Centre in Belgrade in May 1998. I'll take you to the first portion. The first portion is headed "Police operation in Cirez and Likoshane, the 28th of February, 1st of March, 1998."

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you involved in any of the investigations in relation to that?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't involved in the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The second portion, which is on the fifth page, is called the "Police operation in Donji Prekaze, 5th and 6th of March, 1998." Were you involved in any of the investigations leading to this particular report?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I wasn't, not in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The third one is entitled -- and it's on page, "Glodjane, the March Clash and the Aftermath," and it says: "On the basis of its research into the events in Glodjane village from 24 March to 22 April 1998, the HLC registered serious violations in this period of fundamental human rights and international humanitarian law. The statements made to HLC researchers by 28 witnesses, ethnic Albanians, Serbs, and Montenegrins," and so on. Were you involved in the investigation in relation to that particular incident?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And if you can just very briefly - we may have touched on this yesterday - tell the Trial Chamber what your input was into preparing that part of the report.

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I interviewed some of the villagers from the area of Decan.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are those referred to, your interviews, are they referred to in your incident report and in your diaries?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are you -- I'll come back to that in a moment when I have a better copy of the incident reports. Moving on to the next one, I want to take you to the next report, which is in this bundle, which is called "Spotlight Report 27," headed "Kosovo Disappearances in Times of Armed Conflict," 15th of January to the 30th of July, 1998, published by the Humanitarian Law Centre on the 5th of August, 1998." The first section on page 1 of the report refers to -- has a heading called, "Disappearance of Albanians Attributable to the Police." My question is: Were you involved, or did you make any contribution to the compilation of this particular report in relation to point 1?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I have -- I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Next one, number 2, "Disappearances of Serbs Attributable to the Kosovo Liberation Army." Likewise, did you contribute to that?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The third one is entitled, "Disappearances of Albanians Attributed to Kosovo Liberation Army." Did you contribute to that?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I don't recall that that piece of information came from any of my interviews.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Number 4, just underneath that is "Disappearances of Serbs and Roma in Unclear Circumstances." What was your involvement, at all, in relation to that?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have interviewed families of some of the people listed in this section.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And the final one is called "Disappearances of Albanians in Unclear Circumstances." It's labelled or headed number 5. Same question?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall, sir, being involved in any of these interviews. I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay. The documents I need for you to see are still on their way, but I'll take you back to the first "Spotlight" report and the part that you said you contributed to in relation to Glodjane. Can you please go to your incident reports and identify which of those, if they're there, relate to the report by the Humanitarian Law Centre.

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the incidents where I have spoken -- where I spoke to people? Could you guide me as to how to quote them, by witness or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I might, Your Honour, the suggestion that you had made previously with regard to the file number at the top might be not a bad way of doing it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, of course, I do not know whether there are any doubles there, but I hope that -- files usually do not have the same name. Could you say the file always starting with "File," and then for the first one, "e20glodj.doc," if you could refer to them in this way, then I hope we'd be able to follow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I speak now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would be E20Glodj; the next one would be E19; then E10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please quote the full name of the document, because it could be that there's an E19 with some other extension.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So I do understand that you refer to E20Glodj.doc and E19Glodj.doc.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: E19Glodj.doc.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And now you're moving to E10Glodj.doc, as well? --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, E10. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then E4Glodj.doc and E3Glodj.doc.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: For the record, I have a copy with the ERNs on it. I will just read them for the transcript so we don't lose it. E20Glodj has an ERN which is K0577193; E19 has an ERN of K057791; E10 has an ERN the same, 7171; E4, 7209; and E3, 7206.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are there any other relating to Glodjane there?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I could see in here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for our information at this moment, the incident reports are sorted in such a way that they count down from E20 down and then there's a second portion which starts with E23, E22, and E21. These are the last three in this binder. And have you checked those as well, as to whether you drafted them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those are not mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, that's clear. Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If I could take you to the first one you referred to, which is E10, a report of -- I apologise. I just said it in the wrong order. What I actually meant was E20, which is the one on the top. The date of the report is the 27th of April, 1997. The date of the incident is the 22nd of April, 1998, and it refers to a statement by a one Novak Stijovic. Just to make this clear, was that a statement you took from that particular person?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was a statement from Mr. Stijovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And is that recorded in your -- the diaries which are in the court?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are you able to locate within the diaries which one it is?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Only if it would assist the Trial Chamber to go through this exercise in court. I appreciate it should have been done outside court and taken -- her taken straight to it, but it's just a matter of timing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You may proceed. If it confuses too much, we'll intervene. Please proceed. Could you answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could you repeat the question. I'm not sure I understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You have your diaries. There's a copy of your diaries, the English translation, there. If I could take you to the 13th page of the one which has got on the bottom written "Volume 2." That's behind the first green -- the first green pad -- sorry, first green piece of paper. If I could take you to page 13 of that.

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is that the entry in your diary which relates to that incident report?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Can you be a little more exact, what you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's page 13 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Page 13, and then which paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: At the top of the page, it says "Stijovic Novak," and then it says: "On the 22nd of April, 1998" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, the confusion comes from you referred to the first portion after the first green page, and this is the first portion after the second green page, but at least it's clear to us now, because there's a green divider page that's second or third in order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes, I also see that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we've found it. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The next one I want to take you to is E19, which was the next one which you referred to in terms of the incident reports. The date of that incident report -- the making of the report was the 27th of April; 1998; the incident was on the 22nd of April, 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, just for my information.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your last question, I don't think you received an answer, did you? As a matter of fact, your question was --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- "If I could take you to page 13." Then you said: "Is that the entry in your diary which relates to that incident report?" And then we tried to find exactly what page you were referring to, and I think you later on -- only I asked whether the witness had found it; she confirmed that. But to say that an answer was given to your question, I cannot find that. Would you please, then, seek an answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Ms. Andjelkovic, I confused you saying "Yes, I have it, sir," with "Yes, that's mine." Can you confirm or otherwise to the Trial Chamber whether that is a record of a conversation you recorded with Mr. Novak Stijovic on the 27th of April, 1998?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is a translation of that record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Which pages, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The first one.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's pages 13, 14, and 15 of that translation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Do you mean 13, 14, and the first three lines of page 15?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour Judge Hoepfel is completely correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And what was the ethnicity of Mr. Novak Stijovic?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think he has stated his ethnicity, and I don't think that I asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. The next one I want to take you to was the one you mentioned, which was E19, relating to Kostadin Stijovic, in which a statement there says that, "I was taken prisoner in my village Pozar and then taken to their headquarters in Glodjane. My daughter-in-law Milka Stijovic and neighbour Stana Popovic were taken together with me. They searched us and put us in a car. They didn't ask us any questions. When we got to the headquarters in Glodjane, they questioned me and mussed around my cap. I told them I wasn't at war with anyone." Is that at page 15 of the diaries, that particular conversation or statement?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is the translation of the interview that I took from Mr. Kostadin Stijovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where Mr. Kostadin Stijovic refers to "they" taking him prisoner in his village and "taking me to their headquarters in Glodjane," did he tell you who he was referring to?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you have any information which led you to believe or conclude who he was talking about; that is, who "they" were?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, most villagers would just say "they," and they would usually refer to either armed men or to people they didn't know that they would see in villages or around those roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. Of what ethnicity were these armed men?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He doesn't say in this -- in the notes. He doesn't say in the interview notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The next one you referred to was E10, which was ERN K0577171. The report is of the 27th of April, 1998, relating to an incident on the 18th of April, 1998 at the house of Dragoslav Stojanovic, Dubrava, Decani township, in Kosovo. What can you tell the Court about this particular statement and the circumstances of your taking it?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is -- this was an interview with one of the members of Stojanovic family from -- from Decani, village of Dubrava.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could I take you to page 9 of volume 2 of the diaries, that would be notebooks that's behind the second green -- sorry, that's the -- it should be the same one you were looking at a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Page 9, with an ERN heading of 00 -- sorry, U0030624, Stojanovic Mijat, Dragoslav Dubrava. And on pages 9 to 12, it appears to relate to Mr. Mijat Stojanovic. Now, I briefly touched upon this one yesterday. Is that the corresponding diary entry to that incident report?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, pretty much. That is the translation of -- of the interview I took in April 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Now, in that, you refer to -- that is, the diary, you refer to an incident before Easter. Mijat Stojanovic, I take it, was of Serbian ethnicity, that particular name?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I recall, they considered themselves Montenegrins.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: This one refers to an incident in which 10 to 15 soldiers entered his house. They surrendered. The soldiers were hitting D. Who is D? Was that Dragoslav?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, D was short for Dragoslav.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: " They were hitting Dragoslav with their rifle butts and kicking him with their boots. The two of us were ordered to lie down next to Dragoslav. They beat us as well. When Nasim Haradinaj entered, the beating stopped, but they continued." Then it goes on: "The HQ was located at 800, 1 kilometre from there in the house of Nasim Haradinaj, the house which had been deserted since the 90s." What HQ were you or Mr. Stojanovic referring to in that particular diary entry?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to Mr. Stojanovic, that was in UCK HQ.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The next incident you referred to was E4. The report was the 9th of April, 1997, referring to an abduction on the 14th of September, 1997. I'm not interested in that one. Incident 2, the 24th of March, 1998, Dubrava, Decani township in Kosovo, relating to Dragoslav Stojanovic, where he says: "Statement --" where it says: "Statement by Vladimir Stojanovic. It happened on Tuesday, the 24th of March this year," when his brother and mother were in Dubrava. And it refers to -- "in the neighbours' house, five or six rockets were from hand-launchers in the car and blazed at it with machine-guns. The shooting lasted for about 15 minutes. Then the police arrived and came into our yard where they opened fire on the Haradinaj house in which there were OVK," and it says: "HLC note: Serbian acronym for the Liberation Army of Kosovo soldiers." Now, was this the incident at the Haradinaj house on the 24th of March, 1998?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's what it refers to.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If you can go to volume 1, which is the first set of papers in that binder, and go to page 10. Can you identify whether that passage halfway down the page head -- where it says "9th of April, D. Stojanovic," going over from there to --

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is a translation of -- of the interview on page 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The next one you referred to was E3. A report of the 9th of April, 1998 in relation to an incident on the 24th of March, 1998. It's headed: "Statement by Ljubica Stojanovic." And it says: "I wasn't attacked by Albanians up until now. I hope to go back home if I can. Until the police came, I was with them, the Albanians I mean, every day. Ours is the only Serb house in ten villages. They caught my son Dragoslav the end of February. They stopped him, took his pistol, then gave it back ..." And so on. What was -- Mr. Ljubica Stojanovic -- she? Is Ljubica Stojanovic Serbian?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I recall, she considered herself Montenegrin.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay. If you can go to page 11 of the volume I just referred you to, the earlier one, which was volume 1, the very bottom of the page, where it says: "LJ" -- "LJS have been on the land for 75 years. 55 years is printed. They did not attack me. I intended to return there," et cetera, et cetera. Is that the corresponding entry on your diary?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It is a translation of an entry in the -- in the note -- notebooks.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If I can now take you to the second report which we went to before,"Spotlight" report number 2 -- sorry, number 27, and the first part, "Disappearances of Albanians Attributable to the Police," and so on. I want you to perform the same exercise. If you can just maybe tab that one so you don't lose it. Maybe put a yellow sticker on "Spotlight" report number 27. And if you could then go back to the incident reports and just identify from the incident reports any incident reports you contributed to which were used to -- as source material for "Spotlight" report number 27?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understood right, you would like me to link the summary that is in the spot report to the incident reports that I filed; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. I don't see that you have those incident reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are you able to look at the diaries which are in front of you and identify any diary entries which were used as source material for that particular report?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. I just need to refer to -- to a note where I know who I first heard of, about the names of the elderly missing, if you don't mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was Mr. Labovic who first -- who first told me, and from whom I -- I heard first, that there were several elderly people unaccounted for.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honours, I hesitate to interrupt. I'm just a little confused. She said she needed to refer to a note, and I'm trying to figure out what note she's referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was whether you could find any entry in your notebook where you were not able to identify any of the incident reports. Could you guide us to where -- you seem to have found it, you said, with Mr. Labovic, where to find that in your --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right. I shall try to find it in the translation of notebooks. Where I did find it is in the copy of my first statement four years ago. It has --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, which you have not in front of you at this moment, or do you? No, that's fine. It's only -- I'm just seeking confirmation that -- no problem.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have the translation in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think she also may well have her statement in front of her too, and that's what she referenced. I think. I'm not sure. I just don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Andjelkovic, if you have your statement in front of you, you're supposed not to look in any material which you are not instructed to look at. Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Don't apologise. No one ever told you. So it's quite clear. But don't be disturbed about it. We're just trying to get things as good as we can. I can't see from here exactly what you've got in front of you. But I do understand that this name of Mr. -- I think you said --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Uros Labovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that your recollection was refreshed by your first statement. Mr. Re, it's a matter of finding in documents any reference. I'm wondering whether the Defence were earlier guided, and the witness quite clearly, whether there would be any objection against guiding the witness here?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Absolutely not at all. If Mr. Re has the references, I'd be perfectly happy with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps Mr. Re might assist you if he -- if he, at least, can find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: This is where -- actually, where we got to yesterday. That was the page that said "Kidnapped Serbs: Slobodan Radosevic, Milos Radunovic, Milica Radunovic." It's page 17 of the volume 2, which is the second bundle of documents there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you found that, Ms. Andjelkovic? Page 17 in the second subset.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you recall whether you made an incident report in relation to that particular incident -- in relation to what is recorded in your diary there?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I did. I think I -- I filed all the reports at the time. I have not had any access to these reports. Once I file them, they were out of my interest, to be honest. So there must have been a report from my interview with -- with Mr. Labovic as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: May I ask you, in order to verify that, did you make any marking in your diaries or any note about having filed a certain chapter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Unfortunately, no. If I may tell the Chamber, the notes were there for my use; they were never meant for anything else. That's why sometimes there was -- there's just bits and pieces in them, because they were just there for me to jot down things, and then for the interviews, to later transfer them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. We may come back to that later.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can I take you to -- in the "Spotlight" report 27, the section 2, which is entitled : "Disappearances of Serbs Attributable to the Kosovo Liberation Army." Earlier you told the Trial Chamber that you had contributed to or gathered source material for this report. The first portion, 2.1, was "Unknown Fate of Dara and Vukosava Vujosevic and Milovan and Milka Vlahovic of Gornji Ratis." It says: "The Serb inhabitants of Gornji Ratis fled on 21 April when the KLA took control of the area and found refuge at the youth centre in the town of Decani, close to the medieval -- the Visoki Decani monastery." And it goes down: "The Vlahovics' daughter, who left the village with her brother on the 21st of April, told the HLC they tried to return the next day for their parents but were stopped and turned back by KLA members." I want to ask you: What contribution, if any, did you make to that portion of the report?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I talked to some of the villagers from that general area.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And was what they told you consistent with what is written in that portion of the report?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The next one is 2.2, "Unknown Fate of Slobodan Radosevic and Milica and Milos Radunovic of Dasinovac." It says: "The KLA took control of Dasinovac on 22 April. Most Serbs fled the village the day before. Only Slobodan Radosevic, 64, and Milica Radunovic, 59, and her husband Milos, and the Markovic family remained. Radosevic's wife Rosa and their son Stanisa tried to return for Slobodan the next day. They were able to reach the Pozar village where they were stopped at a KLA check-point and taken to the KLA headquarters in Glodjane where they told the HLC Stanisa was physically abused. They were released later that day but were not allowed to go to Dasinovac for Slobodan. Milica and Milos Radunovic were last seen by their son and daughter-in-law on the 22nd of April, when they came home from Decani ..." and so on. What, if anything, did you contribute to that portion of the report?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. Apart from the names that were told by the villagers about people from Ratishe e Eperme and Dasinovac, that nobody knew at that time what happened to them. I also spoke with Radunovics' daughter-in-law, but I can't recall -- it was at a later date. I can't really recall whether it was in May, in Peje, or later on. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It goes on to say: "Relatives have heard that they were buried by the roadside in Glodjane but no one has seen their graves." How did that information come to be put in the report?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Another colleague of mine was talking to some other families, and then also if I -- if I recall, the daughter-in-law of Radunovics said that the family was trying, through some of their neighbours, ethnic Albanian neighbours, or friends, they were trying to find information as to what had happened to the couple, to the old Radunovics, because the family was afraid to go back to the village themselves. But other information may have come from other sources, because this was a compilation, it was -- this was not written by me, obviously. I'm not -- this was written by legal advisors at the HLC.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I have a question that may more appropriately be handled in private session. I want to seek a bit of guidance here. There was the mention of a colleague. I don't know if the colleague is going to be identified. It seems to me it could be either handled perhaps through cross-examination or it might be appropriate for it to be dealt with at this point in time, since the witness is relying on the help from a colleague. But obviously if it's a name of some sensitivity, it's something that I don't -- I don't want to offend anybody's concerns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, I don't know whether I fully understood you, but if the witness would like to refer to any name of colleagues, then you would suggest that I offer to the witness to go into private session. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, only because I believe there may be some hesitancy in that regard, and for the moment I don't know how the Chamber wishes to handle it. I didn't know what you wanted to do, so I thought I'd raise the subject before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Andjelkovic, we dealt with it yesterday as well. If you would have any hesitation as to giving names because you may have some concerns about -- perhaps security concerns, whatever, not having been in a position to consult with the persons you'd like to name, please address me and then we'll consider whether or not to go into private session. But before we do so, I'm also looking at the clock. Mr. Re, I, yesterday, told you that you would have certainly not more than one hour. It's now 60 minutes ago that the witness entered the courtroom. So if I deduce the time we spent on procedural matters before the witness came into court and if I would take into consideration that some, could I call it, confusion time, that it's -- well, I could not find any other party to be blamed for it, let me say it the frank way. Then you've supposed to finish your examination-in-chief in the next eight to ten minutes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Ms. Andjelkovic, I want to take you to point 2.1, which says: "Disappearances of Serbs Attributable to the Kosovo Liberation Army." 2.1: "Unknown Fate of" -- I've said that one, I apologise. Can I take you to 2.24, which is on page 13, which is entitled: "The Abduction of Police" -- sorry, 2.24: "The Abduction of Police Officers Nikola Jovanovic and Rado Popadic." It gives the source as the Belgrade media, but did you have anything to do with the compilation of that report in relation to that particular incident?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you just --

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't interview anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you just identify for the record, in the time available, just by the number, the heading, and the title of the portion of the report that you contributed to. If you just go from the beginning to the end and just read onto the record the bits which you assisted in finding the source material to put into the end product.

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. It would be 2.1 that we've already mentioned, 2.2, 2.5 -- no, sorry, I'm sorry. It's not 5. It's 2.6: "Arbitrary Detention of Three Women from Veliki Djurdjevak," I think is the other name. 2.7, 2.8, 2.10 --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry to rise to my feet at this moment, and I'm not objecting, but it's right that you should know, this report covers a much wider period than the indictment region and the passages that the witness is now referring to are passages that were dealt with in her witness statement which the Prosecution have indicated that, because of their lack of relevance to this trial, they did not propose to introduce. I don't object, but you ought to know that that's the position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Re, I can imagine that you'd rather use your time and perhaps at a later moment respond --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- since there's no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: At the moment I just want the witness to identify those passages. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Keep going, please.

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was 2.11, 2.12, and 2.15. Shall I continue in the last paragraph? All right. In the last section that starts "Disappearances of Serbs and Roma in Unclear Circumstances," it was 4.5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since you read that title from the previous paragraph, could you read that title so we're sure we're on the same paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So it's paragraph 4, Roman (iv): "Disappearances of Serbs and Roma in Unclear Circumstances."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then 4.5 reads?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And then 4.5 reads: "Radomir and Dragutin Vostic from Jelovac."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Any others in this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think so, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Ms. Andjelkovic --

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in this section.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- there are two things I wanted to do before I finish. The first one, I'll ask you some questions, the general -- first of all, I just want you to go through the remainder of the incident reports and identify any others, just by reading the incident number onto the record, that you assisted in compiling. You only went through -- you only identified Glodjane the first time. I just want those on the record and then I want to ask you several questions about your general observations, and that will conclude my examination-in-chief. If you go back to the incident reports, if there's any that you didn't tab or you haven't mentioned before related to Glodjane -- I didn't take you specifically to any others, apart from those in Glodjane.

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see any here.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you've given evidence of visiting Kosovo on a number of occasions as a human rights monitor, interviewing Serbs who told you that they had been displaced from their homes and who had had encounters with armed Albanians and members of the KLA; that's in the incident reports. What did you observe? Was there anything that emerged from what they told you which enabled you to draw any conclusions about what was going on there, based upon your experience, your observations, things you heard, things you saw?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I do apologise. I think Your Honour knows the nature of the concern. This is specifically what, as we understood it, Your Honour had indicated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Mr. Re - I carefully looked at the phrasing of his question - was not asking for the conclusions but just for facts that --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think he asks specifically at line 16 "which enabled you to draw any conclusions ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, he didn't ask what conclusions those were, just whether there were facts which -- that's, at least, how I understand the phrasing.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, Ms. Andjelkovic, you're invited to tell us what you observed and what caught your attention which may have led you to conclusions. We are not at this moment primarily interested in what conclusions you've drawn, but mainly on what observations you made which gave you reason to think about what happened there. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right. So the -- whatever observations I had were -- well, first of all, there was increased tensions in smaller -- smaller places like Decan, or a city in the west, Peje/Pec. There was more police and everybody was very nervous. And then based on my interviews with some of the people from the villages, there was increased fear. And indeed, after Easter that year, what the people I interviewed told me was that most ethnic Serb or Montenegrin villagers had left and went to -- either to bigger towns, like Gjakova or Decan, or someplace else where they had family.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In general, what were the reasons that you were given for their leaving, and where were they leaving?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Villagers that I talked to in the first -- before mid-April, the first that left would usually have small children and so they would want to go to a safer place, they -- the people that I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I stop you for a second.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did they say, My wife left or my family left because they have got small children? Or did you observe that there were small children and you interpreted that as the reason for them leaving? Is that what they told you or was that your own conclusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were two cases that I can recall now, off the top of my head, where people said, I have small children; I can't stay. So that -- and, as I said, at police check-points, the police were quite nervous and there were high tensions. And, indeed, I was stopped on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was your understanding, based on everything you understood and heard in that area of Kosovo in March, April, May of 1998, about what was occurring?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding was that there were armed men somewhere in the villages, in Dukagjin area, and that the two main reasons for the -- from some of the villagers leaving was generally insecurity or the fact later on, around Easter time, that they were stopped by armed men or taken and questioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was your understanding, based on everything you saw and heard in the same period, about who these armed men were?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, could you invite the witness there to -- could you please guide the witness there exactly and sources of knowledge. I mean, understanding is rather vague and could -- I can understand things because my mind allows me to draw conclusions or I can understand things by an analytical approach on the things I see. I would like you to be very precise there. Perhaps I could assist the witness. Ms. Andjelkovic, Mr. Re asks you about who these armed men were. If you answer that question, could you very precisely indicate whether your understanding was based on what was told to you or -- and then preferably also who told you, and then also exactly what they told you. So it's a rather generally phrased question. Could you be as precise as possible in your answer as to your source of -- the basis for your understanding.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I understood from the people that -- that have talked to me, they were afraid of armed groups that spoke Albanian. Some of the villagers that I spoke with were talking about people in uniforms; others were talking about people in civilian clothes but armed. I have to say, I haven't seen anyone. This is only based on what people -- some of the people that I spoke to told me. And there was also what police were saying at check-points.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were they saying -- were they talking about the language the armed men used; are you specifically referring to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, when the police is concerned or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, first. You said what the police were saying.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What the police were saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, you mentioned a few things, whether in uniform, not in uniform, but you also mentioned language. What exactly did the police say in this respect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, in this respect, the police was -- was saying that these people were terrorists. They weren't saying anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Didn't say anything about language, they didn't say --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they weren't say anything. They -- they would always refer with this name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you earlier referred to villagers telling you that they were afraid of people speaking Albanian.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have a recollection on this reference to language? Was that made by all of them, half of them, 10 per cent of them? I'm trying to find out how many people you spoke to mentioned the use of this language when they referred to the armed men.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were a few villagers that I spoke with in Decan right after Easter mentioned the language, and they were spoken to in Albanian but also in Serbian, if they didn't understand. Also, another -- in an -- earlier than that, I don't recall -- I've seen it here, that that interview was translated. A young boy that -- that I spoke with at Peje Hospital also mentioned that a group of people stopped them and that they were armed, and they spoke to them first in Albanian, and then when they didn't understand, they spoke to them in Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you say "a few," what should I understand a few to be, 5, 10, 50?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A few? I would say half a dozen would be the safest bet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On a totality of how many people you spoke to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Throughout the whole period or just in that time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In that time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, in that time. It might have been maybe 20 people in the different villages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, any further questions? Because you had spent already your ten minutes but -- eight to ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I just wish to clarify something from that, if you permit me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That is in relation to the armed men, were you told these armed men were Serbian, military, Serbian police, or someone else?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. When -- when the villagers talked about police, they would always say "the police."

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The ethnicity of those people who were telling you that they were fearing these armed men who weren't Serbian police, et cetera, what was their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, who --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The ethnicity of those who were in fear of the armed men.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most people that I spoke with at that time were referring to themselves as ethnic Serbs or Montenegrins. Predominantly they're Orthodox Christians, but people in Kosova sometimes say that they are Serbs, sometimes Montenegrins.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, may I assume that this concludes your examination-in-chief? Ms. Andjelkovic, where we hoped to finish within one hour, we did not manage to do that. Mr. Emmerson, could you tell us how much time you need to prepare?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I don't think a great deal of time, but there are just one or two matters of practical clarification that I'd like some assistance with from Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: For example, it had been my aim to cross-examine on the material electronically through e-court, rather than to cross-examine from a paper bundle which isn't paginated. But I notice that Your Honours have been making markings during the course of this witness' most recent evidence-in-chief. I'm entirely in your hands. I can -- either way there's going to have to be some delay, because it now appears that Mr. Re has not uploaded this material onto the e-court system, but on the other hand, I don't have it cross-referred to paper sources.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm -- Madam Registrar is also a bit confused about what material to use, et cetera. Perhaps if you could work on the same basis, also in order not to confuse the witness because --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: On the paper basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps exceptionally, this, although being my first e-court case, the start is that -- not that brilliant in that respect. And then, of course, we have to keep a close eye on what material we're using, whether it will be uploaded, et cetera, et cetera, so that we have no confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just two things, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: That necessitates a short period of time to transfer references across.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It also will mean that what could have been a much more efficient cross-examination will take slightly longer because we'll be having to leaf through the bundle, but -- with my apologies to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. How much time do you think you'll need? We'll then schedule the break for the time you would need.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, I can certainly be ready by 5.00. I would hope to be able to be ready before that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps we'll take time until 5.00. That's most convenient for everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, I will certainly be ready by then. And I shan't be, Ms. Andjelkovic can be re-asssured, a very great period of time with her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any further observations by --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I, too, am slightly concerned about how we're going to proceed. At this point, I'm wondering whether or not it might not be -- it might behoove us to, for the moment, generically mark the binder that we all received marked as -- mark for identification purposes only collectively as P3. I'm just trying to figure out some way of dealing with it, because I was going to be examining with regard to P1 and P2, and I just -- I want to make sure that I'm at the right place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that material -- you would like to refer to also in the binder we received today?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I believe that it is, Your Honour. I have to double-check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's perhaps -- Madam Registrar, would it be, although it's -- there are quite some different documents in there, could you perhaps consult with me during the break and see how we are going to number this material at this moment, and the confusion is complete, I agree with you, Mr. Guy-Smith, but let's try to get through it. Mr. Harvey, any ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I will not be doing anything to add to the confusion, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much, Mr. Harvey, for this very useful contribution. We adjourn and we'll resume at 5.00, so we'll have a break of 50 minutes. Ms. Andjelkovic, then you'll be cross-examined by counsel for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Before the cross-examination starts, there was the matter you addressed in private session before. I do have an answer for you. I can probably give it to you in open session, or it wouldn't matter if it was heard --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It depends on the answer, I take it, whether you can -- if you can -- I also have one tiny, little procedural matter which I'd like to deal with also in order to make everyone -- put everyone in the position to proceed with what he has to do. My point would be that there was a confidential motion for videolink. That motion is denied, reasons to follow. That's short. Whether we'll give the reasons orally or in writing is another matter. But we'll try to formulate it as precisely as possible. But for your information, the motion is denied. Yes, the other matter, if you could just be as brief as I was on the matter, then ...

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If I can move into private session for one moment. There's no problem with the witness being here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think I have an inkling of how Mr. Re proposes to approach this, and when I respond to it, I'm going to have to deal with the order of witnesses generally for the next two weeks. And given that that is the -- given that that is the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It might be better to deal with it at the end of the day, unless it's desperately urgent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's deal with it at the end of the day. I further inform you that there's another decision to be delivered. We'll do that also after we've heard the testimony of this witness. Very practically, we have considered the -- well, to say it, the situation at this moment as far as exhibits are concerned. We reviewed the content of the binder of today. We find that there's a provisional translation of notebook 1 in non-ERN sequential order but in the right chronology, order of the original. That's the first portion, apart from a cover page which seems to be unrelated to the matter. That will receive a number. Then we have a draft translation, second notebook, ERN numbers sequential. That will get a number as well. Then there's a third portion in the binder which has not been referred to today, from what I understand, and which is, from what we also understood, a copy of the one originally submitted. That will not get a new number. It has not been referred to today. Then we have -- the next portion is a series of translated incident reports. I'll define them in more detail at a later stage. That will get a new number as well. Then we have another section containing two "Spotlight" reports, and that will get a separate number as well. So we'll have four exhibits in addition today. Since we do not know exactly whether these are the final versions of the notebooks, it might well be that at a later stage, that a chronologically correct version, perhaps a selection - that would be a possibility - but at least those portions completely translated, that they will be tendered and that would finally be the evidence. I mean, the content would exactly be the same. But what's the reason why the Chamber does not want to have these earlier versions replaced? That is because it will be almost impossible, reading the transcript, to know exactly what we're talking about. So it might well be that what is now P1 and P2 and what most likely will be P3 and P4, that they might never be admitted into evidence and only a selection, well translated, well chronological order, finally will be admitted into evidence; that's still to be seen. As far as the series of incident reports, it's more likely that they'll be tendered, and we'll then have to decide whether to admit them in evidence, and the same would be true for the "Spotlight" reports. This is what the Chamber has in mind as far as numbering is concerned at this moment, allowing a full reconstruction of what happened during these days in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I indicate and seek clarification just on one minor matter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Where it has been possible to do so, we have uploaded onto the e-court system and released to the court officer on the public side of the system those documents that I will be using in cross-examination. They are also in the bundle so that we can simultaneously see them on the screen. But they will obviously have a Defence doc. identification -- document identification number as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I suggest that at a later stage, we'll see whether there's any need to have them admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If not, then they're still marked for identification or not admitted. But at least it allows us again to clearly follow what is on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And since the numbering does not interfere because these will all be D numbers, there's no problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But that is not possible, I emphasise, in respect of the notebooks because they have not been uploaded onto the system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
