I'm sorry, the paragraph comes up different on the screen, I'm told. Can you see a paragraph beginning: "Then Nasim Haradinaj turned up again ..."

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. And to summarise the remainder, Nasim Haradinaj, it is said, then took these three men to Baballoq and released them into an area where there was Serb forces; yes?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can we just look at the final paragraph where he describes to you those who were there. "90 per cent of them," he said, "were in uniform and had small arms."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have to move to the next page, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, there we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: "They took their masks off. None of them kept his mask on. They were mostly my neighbours, guys I went to school with, kept company with, shopped in their stores. So I know 95 percent of them. The remaining 5 per cent I didn't recognise because they weren't from our parts." Yes?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So in the course of that interview with Mijat Stojanovic, it is clear, is it not, that he made no suggestion that Ramush Haradinaj took part, or any part, in those events or that he was present?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just heard the name Haradinaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, it may be important to know who we're talking about, because Haradinaj is a very, very common name in that part of the world, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Is it not?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It wasn't Ramush Haradinaj he was talking about, was it? It was perfectly obviously Nasim Haradinaj.

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he said Nasim Haradinaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. And he knew who all of those involved were?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what he claimed, according to the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now finally, if I may, this: Can we look at page 17 of your second notebook, briefly, where you've listed a group -- or the names of what were described there as kidnapped Serbs. You said you got this information from somebody called Uros Labovic; yes?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Uros Labovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just to be clear. You've had a chance to look at your witness statement that you made in this --

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No, please don't apologise. If you weren't asked not to, then it's most certainly not your fault. But in that witness statement you make it quite clear that you never met or spoke to anybody who'd witnessed these people being kidnapped.

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No. And so when you've used the word "kidnapped Serbs" there, I mean, those are your own personal notes, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were -- everybody was talking about kidnappings.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody said abductions or anything else; it was always kidnapping.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But nobody you spoke to had seen abductions or kidnappings.

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding even at the time was -- I mean, this is -- people were talking -- I have -- I think, again, I have to explain. When I was taking notes, I would just find the easiest way --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- to do that, because people were talking sometimes fast and I would just jot down these things. And that's -- you won't find them, you know, nicely phrased. The names seem to have been known by almost everyone because these are small communities, but I did hear them from Mr. Labovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: As people who, at that stage, were unaccounted for?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, would Your Honour just give me one moment? Just the one point that we left outstanding on the notebook, to determine that -- from the original. I don't know whether it's been possible in the meantime to identify that passage in the original notes. We have an ERN number for the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, let's try to find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The ERN number for the page on the original notebook should be U0030210.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we have that on the screen, if possible. It is in P1, so therefore ...

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, there we have it. It might be useful just to look at the previous page first so that the witness can see the context properly. Just at the bottom of the previous page.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Were you able to find the reference to Sacir Bekir?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Perhaps we can move to the following page so the witness can see it, the top of the following page.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Do you have that there?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, do you know, looking at the context, the word in brackets, what is that?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, it says -- it says "stiganin," that was verbatim. It means gypsy. That's how they called the man.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So someone was referring to that man in a derogatory way?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Someone was referring to a Roma. I don't know whether --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They went it derogatory because that used to be quite common way of referral, and it stayed in some areas --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But it's not --

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- especially amongst the less educated people.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It's not your language, though? It's not you putting that?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It's what someone said to you?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Exactly. So my question is: What were you being told is the significance of Sacir Bekir? Is that the man who was the neighbour that is being referred to?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You can't say?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Really, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Is there any other that you can see, looking at it in context, as the author of it, can you see any other reason why you might have referred to that Roma gentleman in the middle of a passage about a neighbour?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Really, I can't. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well. No. Thank you very much, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I am looking at the clock at this moment. I would first like to find out whether, and how much time, other Defence counsel would intend to use for cross-examination. I say this because we've spent now approximately one and a half hours when the initial assessment when I think all three counsel was, I think, one hour and 15 minutes. So therefore my scheduling is a bit disturbed. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm assuming we're not taking any further breaks?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we have to take a break anyhow because we'll have to -- I mean, we have to change tapes. We can't run on two hours for tapes. And the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I believe -- I believe that I could complete my examination, as I indicated before, I think I said it was within 15 or 20 minutes. I believe I can still do the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I shall be surprised if I have any questions at all for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I know how difficult it is, Mr. Re, to give an assessment on how much -- whether you would, at this moment, intend to re-examine the witness, and how much time that would take, not having heard all of the cross-examination. Could you give us an indication?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There's only one thing I wish to ask in clarification at the moment, but there's one other matter I wish to raise, and that is we have another witness outside in the witness room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, certainly today there's no chance. I mean, we can continue until 7.00. I wonder even whether we can finish your examination today or whether we need a little bit more time. Much depends on you, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour, and if I might be of any assistance, I have two areas of examination. I know precisely what questions I wish to ask in each area. I'm going to ask to go into private session for about 30 seconds to make sure that no names are violated, and I may well be able to do it even quicker. I will do my best to get it done by the end of this evening, depending how long a break we take.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The problem is that for some rest, of course, the earlier break was a bit longer, what would be the minimum time we could use for a break? Would that be 15 minutes, Madam Registrar? Keeping in mind that we had a break of 50 minutes earlier. Because I have a bad reputation already to continue after 7 and I would want to confirm that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have to ask the interpreters. I think the tape, as such, would not create major problems. At the same time, I don't want to continue without giving you sufficient rest. Mr. Guy-Smith, do you think you could finish in ten minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Hope springs eternal, but I don't want to commit to ten.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm asking the interpreters whether they would strongly oppose against continuing. You have one escape and that is from now on, in 28 minutes, the tape will be over, so you are not at risk to go beyond 7.00. At the same time, I know that it's much asked from you. I'd like to have an honest response, and I don't want you to be forced into any situation which you'd like not to be in.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is no problem for the interpreters to continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Guy-Smith, you also know that we're running out of the tape if we take too much time, and then that means that we couldn't finish today. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, if we could briefly go into private session for one second.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Please proceed, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just so we're all clear here, when you used the term "police," you are referring to Serbian police, are you not?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the so-called Ministry of the Interior, or MUPs, as they were called.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: MUPs.

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: There were no Albanian police during that time in that period, in that region; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot claim that, sir. I haven't met any, but I can't say if there were or there were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we could get up on the screen, please, that would be P6, which is the "Spotlight" report number 26, and I'm going to be referring to page 13, and the information which is above number 4, "Lull Before the Fresh Clash."

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P6 is not yet uploaded in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Then 1D978 - and I do apologise, Madam Registrar - page 13.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: On page 13 of that report, there is the following information: "Word came to Gramacelj of the attack on neighbouring Glodjane. Teachers dismissed their classes and some 300 children found themselves on the road just as a column of police vehicles, armoured personnel carriers, pinzgauers, and trucks was passing. 14-year-old NV says he was terrified when four vehicles split off from the column and headed toward the children." And then there's some italicised information there: "The police held their guns aimed at us. We screamed, thinking they were going to kill us. We scattered into the nearby streets. The younger kids kept going around in circles, they were so scared, they didn't know where to run, and they were crying. I was awfully scared and thought I'd never get home. As soon as the police column had passed through Gramacelj, many villagers fled their homes to seek refuge with relatives in neighbouring villages." Do you see that passage?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, is that passage, if you know, is that passage a passage that comes from information that was obtained from the individual we were talking about before, person A, involving e21glodj.doc, which is a report of the 30th of March, 1998?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would appear so. If it is under those initials, it would appear so.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: If you can turn your attention to the second page, please. And I believe the language that's contained in the report that I just read, that "Spotlight" report number 26, which is language which is the part of the second full paragraph on the second page of the report, starting with "There are about 300 kids in the school."

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It goes on, and the report also indicates -- and I'm now referring to the very last paragraph. It says: "Three days before the attack on Glodjane, three Nivas, one black and two white, came to our village. There were five policemen in each of the white cars and they held their automatic rifles sticking out of the windows. In the black Niva there were five men wearing masks, black wool stockings, and they had automatic rifles. They stopped at the school. Only the masked men got out of their car. They wore black uniforms with white eagles on the sleeves." Do you see that information? It goes on.

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Did you ever get any further information about masked men with white eagles on their sleeves?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Referring your attention for the moment to the other report compiled by your colleague, which I believe is E5, it seems that the same language is there too, or the same concern. In this one, it goes a bit further, because it says: "In the black jeep there were five masked men in black uniforms with white eagles on one sleeve. One had a camera and took pictures of the village. I saw it with my own eyes."

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Did you ever, in the terms of the work that you were doing, did you ever get any further information about these masked men?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And I take if the reason for that would be because you were -- you were dealing with, as you told Mr. Emmerson, you were dealing with the Serb -- with the Serbian aspect of the interview process.

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At that time, mainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Both of the documents that I have referred to Your Honours, I believe, are contained in what has been presently marked as P5.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm going to turn away from that and ask you questions in another area. Do you recall yesterday that Mr. Re asked you about the killing of a gentleman, I believe his name was Prascevic --

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prascevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Prascevic, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prascevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Prascevic, thank you very much. And during the time that you were involved in that particular interview, you had a couple of interviews concerning the death of that gentleman; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: What date was that?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was -- I think that was the beginning of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: What you learned - and this is information that you learned personally; this wasn't something that you heard through rumour or gossip or many people said, but personally, not somebody telling you - you learned that Mr. Prascevic had a relationship with an Albanian woman who had betrayed him in order to save his own neck; right?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That seems to be the case, but it was a very -- I was never quite clear about this story.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me ask you this: I'm referring now to the translation of your notes. It would be -- I believe now it's been marked as Prosecution 3, 19 of the translation. That's in the binder again, very beginning. That would be blue notebook, volume 1. And it's going to be the -- and I'm taking my cue from Judge Hoepfel. It's one, two, three lines down. That was the information that you learned, I believe, from Mr. Prascevic's wife. Page 19, going down one, two, three lines. Do you see it there?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you also learned that Mr. Prascevic had been suspended. He was a police officer and he had been suspended from his job; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And as a matter of fact, "he," that is Mr. Prascevic, "had apparently threatened to kill the chief," and I take it by that you mean chief of -- his chief, the chief of police. I'm referring now to page 20, the next page over, and that would be the top of the page and that would be the first and second page of the top of the page in terms of the --

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Right? Okay. Now, before you went on this mission, did you have any information concerning the fact that, as a general rule, the Serbian police, the MUP, as you've called them, were in the process of taking weapons away from Albanians, plain old Albanians living on their land?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that I'd heard something reported by one of my colleagues. There was -- I don't remember the names of villages, but there were families whose houses were searched for weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And that was back --

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I can't remember. It was in the Dukagjin area. I can't -- I really don't know. Those were not my interviews. So I know it was right about that time, but I can't remember the names of villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Okay. And I think -- I think I'm going to be able to do it even a bit quicker than I thought. I have only one last question for you, and that's if you could be with me on this: You learned that that woman, the Albanian woman, "was betraying Albanians, she was betraying her own family, and that he," and I take it by that you mean Mr. Prascevic, "took many weapons from them," that would be her own family, I guess, and others, "and he received information from her. However, her husband died last summer. He was murdered." That's what you were told; right?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I can't -- are we --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: That would be page 29. We're still in the same blue notebook, volume 1. I do apologise for the cumbersome way I'm doing this, but we're in paper. And that would be the one, two -- that would be the third full paragraph where it says: "Wife ..."

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, his wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, you never received any information as to whether or not, whether -- put it another way, as to who killed Mr. Prascevic, did you?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, again, I was a police detective -- I wasn't a police detective to learn that and to investigate.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I understand. And during that period of time, if I'm not mistaken, the Albanian woman, she was shot, too; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She claimed that she was shot and indeed I did talk to her at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Were you able to verify or substantiate that claim?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot really, because I went to the hospital and I talked to her. There was somebody translating for me, but I can't -- I can't really recall who. But I seem to -- I seem to remember that there was somebody sitting next to me - I really can't recall who that was -- because the woman did not speak Serbian very well, and at that time I still -- I still can't speak Albanian, but at least I can understand and, you know, read the newspaper and understand what people are saying. At that time I couldn't; this was early March.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Understood.

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I talked through somebody who was interpreting for me, but I can't remember who, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You did the best you -- you did the best you could with what you had.

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your time and your patience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith. Mr. Harvey, have you changed your mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, no surprises.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No surprises.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then before ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before I give an opportunity to Mr. Re to ask his clarifying question in re-examination, Judge Hoepfel would like to put a question to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Just to give us a complete picture of your diaries or notepads, it was asked if all notepads are at the court, in the possession of the court, and maybe I can ask you: There were four notepads put to the Court. Is that the number of notepads you remember?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. That is the number I remember. There may have been interviews that were recorded elsewhere, on a piece of paper, that went into the HLC files; but these were all the notebooks that I had and that is what I gave -- again, I don't remember quite when, but I gave to an OSCE colleague, who was actually my immediate supervisor when I was with the Kosovo Verification Mission, and she had them in her came and gave them to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. So you cannot give us an idea when, about, it was first undertook to translate portions of these diaries?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. I have no idea. I only know that I was contacted by the Tribunal in, I think, the year 2002. So I don't know what was happening with them in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. To have an idea of the process, then, it appears that there are some markings or some notes every now and then. For example, let us see the original, which is ERN number U0030320. But it appears all over these texts, and they seem not to have been included in the translation so I suppose they were added later and maybe by a different person or by several persons. Can you give us some idea about that? Do we have it already?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Am I supposed to look at the screen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Will the screen show this page? Yes. Do you have it on the screen, your handwriting, this page?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: And after some lines, it comes "Otoc," and then you see above this line this "NNLOKAN2.doc" and then there's a double U, a sign, two ticks. Do you remember what that was? Normally it was framed, like in a box.

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Can you explain that to us, because --?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't quite remember when, but sometime probably in the autumn of 1998, at the HLC, we were told how to file the document so that it would -- they would be correctly filed and always have the same -- follow the same pattern. And the "NN" -- I think that the "NN" here means that the person did not want to be named. And then the second thing, that was the name of the village. And then number 2 after this "LOCAN" would be the number of the interview taken. And that would follow -- that pattern was followed through. So it didn't matter who took the interview. It would just always be where it was from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: So it would then be part of a computer document.

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes. Sometimes there is added, or often, "MA"; this would be your initials, I suppose?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they would.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Okay. So we now understand a little more of the methodology and how this came about. Thank you. This was my only question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, you said you needed to put one clarifying question, at least that was the situation a quarter of an hour ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It was a clarifying --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please put the question, because we're running out of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Earlier, Mr. Emmerson asked you about displacements in the -- he asked you about the police attack on the village of Glodjane, and at page 85 you said: "There were times when people would be displaced because there was shooting and there was an incident, and then when things calmed down, they would come back. That was the pattern for quite a few months in Kosovo overall." That was the answer you gave. When you gave that answer, were you referring to people of the Serbian ethnicity or another ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I recall was that was -- that was the case with both communities in some cases. And the first thing off the top of my head is, for example, Orahovac, which happened a bit later, and it's a bit more -- a bit central Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I just want to try to focus this. When you were talking about that, were you talking generally or were you talking about the Serbian or the Albanian? If you could answer that in a word or two, it would assist.

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say I was talking -- I was referring to civilian population, not particularly to ethnicities.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The second part of my clarification is: When you said that was the pattern -- sorry, you said: "When things calmed down, they would come back. That was the pattern for quite a few months in Kosovo overall." My next clarifying question is: Did that change and -- did the pattern change to permanent displacements?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did, in those places where villages were burned or houses were burned.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And what areas were those?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You would have to be really specific, at what time, because the conflict spread.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just to make it relevant to this indictment, does that refer to any of the incidents or the places you referred to in your notebook or the report, that is, permanent displacements?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean in the time period that --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that you are interested in?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that I have any reference that it was permanent in my notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about your knowledge? You referred to a situation where -- when things would calm down and people would come back, and your knowledge, based upon your going to those villages and those areas, did there come a time when there were permanent displacements?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall that people I spoke with in Decan in April, I cannot recall that they went back to their villages. But, again, at that time we couldn't, obviously, say whether that was permanent or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You're saying at that point it wasn't permanent --

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In April, in April of 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any need for further questions by the Defence? I see three times nodding no. Since the Bench has no further questions for you, Ms. Andjelkovic, this concludes your testimony. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague to testify before this Court and for answering questions of both parties and the Bench, and also for having to undergo all logistical problems we faced these days. Thank you very much. Madam Usher will escort you out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, for being patient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At this moment there's no further time for procedural issues. We're running out of tape. The only thing I'd like to say is that the Chamber has considered the request for protective measures and the request is granted, reasons to be given when we are not running out of tape. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There was the issue of the timing you asked me about earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I can give you the answer in seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: CLSS has a turnaround of two hours for issuing -- for translating documents issued by the Chambers. And there are no travel documents. The situation of 24 hours still goes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would there be any problem, as far as the Defence is concerned, that Chamber staff and Prosecution would communicate as to any practical problems in this respect? Then, Mr. Re, that will take place and we'll not cause any further delay in a decision on the matter. We stand adjourned until tomorrow, Courtroom II, quarter past 2.00.
